description: Full-stack developer (20+ years) from Santa Cruz, Bolivia, leading the tech side of our Field Shift project: using NASA data to help farms adapt to a changing climate. I ship working prototypes fast and I also do photography and podcasts. Looking for designers, artists and people who know agriculture (farmers, agronomists, students) to make satellite data simple and useful for farmers. No coding needed. Spanish or English welcome.
summary:
GrazePoint tells a rancher when each paddock is ready to graze. At Hacienda Patiño in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, that call is made today by a technician's trained eye, walking the fields.

The app turns that eye into a number. A farmer draws their ranch on a satellite map, records what they know (pasture species, last grazing date, herd size, lab soil results) and GrazePoint crosses it with NASA data: daily weather from POWER, pasture health every 8 days from MODIS NDVI via GIBS, root-zone moisture from SMAP L4 and soil properties from SoilGrids/ISRIC.

It answers with decisions, not dashboards: which paddock hits its grazing point, how many days of forage the herd has left, what to plant next and when. The report goes out over WhatsApp, alerts arrive on Telegram and a technical PDF documents the method.

Open source, runs in the browser, works for any ranch the satellites pass over.
details:
GrazePoint is a web tool that answers the question a cattle rancher asks

every morning: which paddock should the herd enter today, and which ones

need rest, cutting, or reseeding. We built it around a real case. At

Hacienda Patiño in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, that call is made by eye, walking

the field, by a technician with years of experience. We interviewed the

ranch's director the day before the hackathon and designed the tool

against her answers.

How it works: you draw your farm's paddocks on a satellite map (or import

them), register what you know (forage species, last grazing date, herd

size, soil lab results), and the app crosses that with open satellite

data. Each paddock gets a re-growth clock: days since last use, weighted

by the water and heat it actually had, so a dry cold week counts less

than a wet warm one. Satellite vegetation index (NDVI) then confirms the

recovery or flags a disagreement worth checking. The output is a ranking:

which paddock is at its optimal grazing point, how many days until the

next one is ready, which grass has gone past maturity, and a planting

window analysis for reseeding. Reports go out as a PDF over WhatsApp,

the channel the field crew already uses.

Benefits and intended impact: it turns the trained eye of one technician

into a number anyone can check from a phone, measured on their own land

rather than a regional average. The immediate beneficiaries are real:

Fundación Patiño trains over 300 producers a year and supplies certified

seed to 1,342 producers across seven departments, and the ranch itself

runs on rotational grazing. Beyond that network, the tool works for any

ranch the satellites pass over, for free, because every input is open

data.

Tools and stack: a bilingual (English/Spanish) browser app in HTML, CSS

and vanilla JavaScript with Leaflet maps, backed by a Node.js REST API at

/api/grazepoint with a mirrored offline backend, PDF report generation,

and WhatsApp/Telegram delivery. NASA datasets: POWER daily API (rainfall,

temperature, top and root-zone soil wetness), SMAP L4 root-zone soil

moisture, and MODIS NDVI served through GIBS. Because soil and crop data

are not NASA products, we add open partner sources: SoilGrids via WCS,

Open-Meteo soil layers, and the ranch's own lab analyses and biomass

measurements.

What makes it creative: the effective re-growth days model, a clock the

rancher can read instead of raw indices, and NDVI treated as a referee

that can disagree with the clock, with the disagreement shown as

information instead of hidden. We also turned a data gap into a feature:

Bolivia has no public parcel or rotation data, so the app says so plainly

and uses vegetation history as the proxy.

Factors we considered: field connectivity and devices (WhatsApp first,

PDF over dashboard), adoption cost (registering a grazing event takes

three taps), honest uncertainty (global grids are coarse in the Andes and

tropics, so we show ranges and warn when a paddock is smaller than the

250 m pixel), and scientific validity (the model infers maturity, a proxy

for lignification, not protein content, and the report says so).
